transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. What brings you to see me today?

Well, hi there doc. I guess what brings me in is... I just keep messing up these little things lately. Like, the other day I was signing up for this class down at the senior center, and I wrote down the completely wrong time on the sheet. Which is a shame because they just remodeled the whole lobby area there where they keep the bulletin board. Used to have this awful green shag carpet, probably been there since 1974, and now it's this nice laminate flooring. My buddy Frank swears it's real oak, but I worked at a hardware store right out of high school, so I know laminate when I see it. 

But anyway, yeah, just making mistakes. Like working out in the garage—I was measuring a board the other day, measured it once, and I still cut it a hair short because I just skipped right over the small print on the plans. It was supposed to be for a birdhouse. My granddaughter loves birds... she's seven now, lives out in Ohio. The state bird there is the cardinal, you know. Beautiful red feathers. But... wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, why I'm here. Just... yeah, missing the small details on things like that.
Have you struggled with attention and missing details throughout your life, or did this start recently?

Oh, no, it's not a new thing at all. It's been going on my whole life, I suppose. I remember my mother used to keep all my old report cards in this big tin box—used to be a Ritz cracker tin, you know the big round ones? They don't make them like that anymore, now it's all flimsy cardboard that gets crushed in the pantry if you put a can of beans on top of it. 

But she kept that tin in the hall closet, and even way back in elementary school, my teachers were writing the exact same things in those reports. They'd say I was a bright boy, but I was always forgetting my textbooks, losing my homework somewhere between the front door and my desk... and I'd just sit there staring out the window all day unless someone was right there to keep me on track. Usually I was watching the school janitor, Mr. Higgins. He had this old John Deere riding mower. Beautiful machine. Classic green and yellow paint job. My neighbor bought a new John Deere just last summer, but it's not the same engine quality, you know? All the parts are plastic now, they just snap if you look at 'em wrong. I told him he should've looked for a used one, but people just want shiny and new. 

But, uh... yeah, so my teachers definitely noticed I was missing things way back when I was a little kid.
